set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: A 78-year-old man fell in the bathroom at 3 a.m. while urinating standing up, after two beers the evening before. He felt a swimmy head, nausea and sweating first and recovered quickly. His vital signs, neurologic examination and glucose are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Situational reflex syncope
Correct. Nocturnal voiding after abruptly rising triggers an exaggerated autonomic reflex, and alcohol and relative dehydration add to it; this is micturition syncope.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows emotional stress, fear, pain, heat or prolonged standing rather than a bodily function such as urination.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension causes a sustained postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not a reflex tied to voiding.
Hypoglycemic loss of consciousness
Hypoglycemia is a non-hypotensive cause of syncope, and his normal glucose rules it out.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 25-year-old woman fainted once after standing for an hour in the heat at a graduation, with warmth and nausea first and rapid recovery. Her examination and readings are normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Begin midodrine daily
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is not first-line for a vasovagal faint.
Advise avoiding the trigger
Correct. Vasovagal syncope is treated by trigger avoidance, here prolonged standing in the heat, with safety precautions when unavoidable.
Start fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, which her normal readings do not suggest.
Refer for echocardiography
Echocardiography is for structural cardiogenic syncope; a triggered faint with a prodrome points to a reflex cause.

set1.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman in a clinic has hypotension from a suspected overwhelming infection and is awaiting transfer. Which therapy should not be started in the clinic?
opts: Arranging urgent transfer
Arranging transfer is appropriate, because the drugs her hypotension may need are used only in the emergency department and intensive care.
Repeating her vital signs
Repeated readings are appropriate, since each reading is only a snapshot in time.
Reviewing her medications
Reviewing medications is appropriate, since medication-mediated hypotension is treated by reducing the offending drug.
A norepinephrine infusion
Correct. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension asks whether she can keep a vasopressor at home for bad days. What should she be told?
opts: Pressors are hospital-only drugs
Correct. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.
A home supply is reasonable
Pressors are not outpatient drugs; home options for neurogenic syncope are midodrine or droxidopa with slow position changes.
Only if she avoids salt
Salt is not the issue; pressors are used only in the emergency department and intensive care.
Only after a tilt-table test
A tilt-table test is for the tachycardia syndrome and would not make a pressor safe for home use.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 70-year-old man has had diarrhea and poor oral intake for 3 days and fainted when he stood up quickly this morning. His oral mucous membranes are dry. Supine he is 134/76 with a heart rate of 66; standing he is 104/62 with a heart rate of 94. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Correct. A 30 mmHg systolic fall with a heart rate rise from 66 to 94 shows an intact sympathetic reflex, and diarrhea with poor intake explains the volume depletion.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension shows only a minimal heart rate rise and usually no volume depletion, the opposite of his findings.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope follows a bodily function such as nighttime urination, with a transient reflex rather than a sustained fall on standing.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia
That syndrome is a heart rate rise on standing without the pressure fall that meets orthostatic criteria; he has a clear 30 mmHg fall.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: A 31-year-old man lost consciousness at work. Coworkers saw rhythmic jerking of all four limbs, he bit his tongue and was incontinent, and he remained confused for 30 minutes. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: A seizure
Correct. Tongue biting, incontinence and prolonged confusion afterward point to seizure, a non-hypotensive cause; syncope ends in rapid, spontaneous recovery.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope is transient and self-limited, with rapid recovery rather than prolonged confusion.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope follows a bodily function such as urination and recovers quickly without prolonged confusion.
Orthostatic hypotension
Orthostatic syncope follows standing and recovers spontaneously; tongue biting and prolonged confusion point elsewhere.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 69-year-old man reports lightheadedness and dimming vision within a minute or two of standing, which settles when he sits. His examination at rest is normal. Which test should be performed first?
opts: A tilt-table test
The tilt-table test is the listed test for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and its sensitivity of about 40% makes a negative result weak.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope; symptoms that follow standing call first for a postural pressure measurement.
A stress test
A stress test belongs to the arrhythmia work-up of cardiogenic syncope, not the first test for a postural pattern of symptoms.
Orthostatic vital signs
Correct. Pressure and heart rate taken supine and again within 3 minutes of standing show whether orthostatic criteria are met and which type the heart rate response suggests.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: A 71-year-old woman with a known cardiomyopathy has had two faints on exertion. Her electrocardiogram shows no arrhythmia. Which test best evaluates a structural cause?
opts: A blood glucose level
Glucose excludes hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, but does not image the heart's structure.
An episode log
A log supports reflex syncope; exertional faints with a cardiomyopathy need cardiac imaging.
An echocardiogram
Correct. Structural causes, infarction, cardiomyopathy, heart failure and valve disease, are evaluated with echocardiography or stress echocardiography plus cardiology consultation.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not the evaluation of a cardiomyopathy.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: A 68-year-old woman with coronary disease felt her heart race and then collapsed without warning in a store. She has recovered and is stable in the office. Which test should be obtained first?
opts: An electrocardiogram
Correct. A suspected arrhythmia is investigated first with an electrocardiogram, then monitoring, a stress test and cardiology consultation.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is listed for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not for a suspected arrhythmia.
An episode log
An episode log supports the history in reflex syncope; palpitations before an abrupt collapse call for a rhythm tracing.
Orthostatic vital signs
Orthostatic readings look for a postural fall; her abrupt collapse with palpitations points to the heart rhythm.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease reports lightheadedness and dimming vision within minutes of standing and fainted once in his kitchen. He is well hydrated. Supine he is 138/80 with a heart rate of 68; standing he is 106/70 with a heart rate of 70. What is the most likely cause of his syncope?
opts: Autonomic failure from Parkinson disease
Correct. Parkinson disease is an example cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and a large pressure fall with almost no heart rate rise marks autonomic failure.
Volume depletion from poor intake
Volume depletion drives a significant compensatory heart rate rise and is usually visible on examination; he is well hydrated with a flat heart rate.
A vasovagal reflex on standing
A vasovagal reflex follows emotional or physical triggers and is transient, rather than a reproducible fall each time he stands.
A ventricular arrhythmia
An arrhythmia causes abrupt collapse, often with palpitations and a fast rhythm, rather than symptoms that build after standing.

set1.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set1.q: A 76-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction heart failure has run low pressures for a year and asks whether his low pressure will simply go away. What is the most accurate answer?
opts: It always resolves within weeks
Chronic hypotension persists and waxes and wanes rather than resolving within weeks.
It needs a vasopressor at home
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not home management of chronic hypotension.
Its cause may not be removable
Correct. Chronic hypotension waxes and wanes, and its underlying cause, here heart failure, may be unavoidable, unlike an acute trigger that can be removed.
It will end once a trigger is found
Removing a trigger fits acute or reflex hypotension; chronic cardiogenic hypotension may have an unavoidable cause.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 72-year-old man has diabetic autonomic neuropathy and also congestive heart failure. He faints on standing. Which of the following should be avoided?
opts: Treating the underlying cause
Treating the underlying condition is the central principle for orthostasis and is never avoided.
A careful history
History is the most important part of diagnosing the source of orthostatic syncope and is always appropriate.
Fludrocortisone
Correct. Fludrocortisone causes salt and water retention and is avoided in congestive heart failure, even though it is best with the tachycardia syndrome.
Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line for orthostatic syncope and are safe alongside heart failure.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: An 80-year-old man takes an alpha-1 blocker and lisinopril and has fainted twice while urinating at night after rising abruptly from bed. His examination and electrocardiogram are normal. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Admit for a vasopressor infusion
Vasopressors are reserved for the emergency department and intensive care for shock, not for a recovered reflex faint.
Order a tilt-table test urgently
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and does not address his reflex triggers.
Reduce contributing medications
Correct. An alpha-1 blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor predisposes to micturition syncope, and iatrogenic contributors are reduced or removed.
Start midodrine for reflex syncope
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is not listed for situational reflex syncope.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 72-year-old man with diabetic autonomic neuropathy takes midodrine but still has lightheadedness on standing. He has no supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat). Which addition is most appropriate?
opts: Phenylephrine at home
Phenylephrine is a pressor used only in the emergency department and intensive care, never as a home medication.
Strict fluid restriction
Restricting fluid lowers volume and worsens orthostatic symptoms; it is not an add-on treatment.
Vasopressin in clinic
Vasopressin, like the other pressors, is reserved for the emergency department and intensive care.
Droxidopa as an adjunct
Correct. Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is usually used as an adjunct with midodrine or fludrocortisone rather than on its own.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with Parkinson disease has neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). Which medication is best suited to her?
opts: Phenylephrine
Phenylephrine is among the pressors used only in the emergency department and intensive care, not an outpatient drug.
Vasopressin
Vasopressin is reserved for the emergency department and intensive care and has no place in outpatient orthostatic care.
Droxidopa
Correct. Droxidopa has mild efficacy but is better with supine hypertension, the setting in which midodrine is avoided.
Midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope in general but is avoided with supine hypertension, which she has.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman with 20 years of type 2 diabetes has fainted twice shortly after getting out of bed. Her mucous membranes are moist, and vibration and light-touch sensation are reduced in both feet. Supine she is 140/80 with a heart rate of 70; after 3 minutes standing she is 110/66 with a heart rate of 74. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Correct. The systolic fall of 30 mmHg meets the criterion, the heart rate barely rises, and long-standing diabetes with neuropathy points to diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
The non-neurogenic form shows a significant heart rate rise from an intact autonomic reflex and usually volume depletion; she has neither.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear, pain or heat with a transient reflex, not a reproducible postural fall on standing.
Cardiogenic arrhythmic syncope
An arrhythmia typically causes abrupt collapse without warning and often palpitations; her faints follow standing, with a regular exam.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 78-year-old man with diabetic autonomic neuropathy also has congestive heart failure. His family asks what could raise his standing pressure. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line for orthostatic syncope and are safe to use alongside heart failure.
Treating the cause
Treating the underlying condition is the central principle for orthostasis and is never something to avoid.
Fludrocortisone
Correct. Fludrocortisone causes salt and water retention and is avoided in congestive heart failure, whatever its benefit in the tachycardia syndrome.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa is a mild adjunct that is better with supine hypertension; heart failure is not a reason given to avoid it.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: A 73-year-old man has a faint while urinating at night, with nausea and sweating beforehand and quick recovery. Which test is used to exclude a cardiac dysrhythmia?
opts: Orthostatic vital signs
Orthostatic readings look for a postural pressure fall; the rhythm is assessed with an electrocardiogram.
An electrocardiogram
Correct. A normal electrocardiogram lowers suspicion of a dysrhythmia, just as a normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia and blood tests address infection.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and does not show the cardiac rhythm.
A blood glucose level
A blood glucose excludes hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, rather than a dysrhythmia.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 26-year-old woman with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome remains symptomatic despite increasing her water and salt intake. She has no heart failure. Which medication is most appropriate?
opts: Norepinephrine
Norepinephrine is a pressor used only in the emergency department and intensive care.
Fludrocortisone
Correct. Fludrocortisone is best with the syndrome; because it causes salt and water retention it is avoided only in heart failure, which she does not have.
Midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope rather than with the tachycardia syndrome.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is an adjunct, better with supine hypertension, not the drug best suited here.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set1.q: A 15-year-old boy has lightheadedness on standing. Within 10 minutes his heart rate rises from 68 to 102, and his pressure is unchanged. Does this meet the heart rate criterion for his age?
opts: No; his rate must exceed 150
The absolute rate criterion is exceeding 120 beats per minute, not 150; his case turns on the adolescent threshold of 40.
No; adolescents need a rise of 40
Correct. His rise of 34 would exceed the adult threshold of 30, but in adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute.
Yes; the rise exceeds 30 per minute
More than 30 is the adult threshold; adolescents need a larger rise of 40, which he does not reach.
Yes; any rise with symptoms counts
The definition uses numeric thresholds within 10 minutes of standing, and symptoms alone do not meet it.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 64-year-old man is recovering from a stomach virus that left him eating and drinking little. He fainted on standing, and orthostatic readings show a large pressure fall with a brisk heart rate rise. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Start a daily midodrine tablet
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; his intact heart rate response points to volume loss, which is treated at its cause.
Restrict salt until he recovers
Salt restriction would not help volume depletion; the aim is to correct the underlying fluid loss.
Expect the faints to be permanent
Volume depletion is a removable cause; once intake recovers the postural fall is expected to resolve.
Keep up fluids while intake is poor
Correct. Poor intake and dehydration are listed causes of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and treating the underlying cause, here the volume loss, is the aim.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent faints with a prodrome, but after a careful history the source is still uncertain. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Begin midodrine empirically
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; starting it without a diagnosis treats a guess rather than the cause.
Refer to the right specialty
Correct. History is the most important portion of diagnosing reflex syncope, or of referring to the right specialty for confirmation when it stays uncertain.
Start a vasopressor at home
Vasopressors are reserved for the emergency department and intensive care and would not clarify the source.
Tell her the faints are harmless
An uncertain source needs confirmation rather than reassurance, because treatment targets the real diagnosis.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 70-year-old man with orthostatic hypotension keeps standing up quickly despite being told not to, because he does not see why it matters. Which approach most improves his adherence?
opts: Explain why the pressure falls
Correct. Understanding is the key to compliance: once a patient knows why the pressure falls on standing, slow position changes make sense and are followed.
Add a vasopressor at home
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care only and do not address adherence.
Repeat the same instruction
Repeating an instruction without the reason rarely changes behavior; understanding is what drives compliance.
Stop discussing it with him
Dropping education abandons the most important tool; patient education is central to managing hypotension.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 60-year-old woman has vomited for 2 days, has dry mucous membranes, and fainted on standing; her heart rate rises from 70 to 98 as her pressure falls 30 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Start midodrine for autonomic failure
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; a brisk heart rate rise shows her autonomic reflex is intact.
Order a tilt-table test first
Tilt-table testing belongs to the tachycardia syndrome; her diagnosis is already clear from orthostatic readings.
Refer her for an echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope, which nothing in her history suggests.
Treat the underlying volume loss
Correct. Her intact heart rate response and dryness point to volume depletion, and orthostasis is managed by treating the underlying condition.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 69-year-old man had a large blood loss after surgery 2 days ago and now feels faint on standing. His pressure falls 30 mmHg with a heart rate rise from 72 to 100. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Order a tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and would delay treatment of an evident volume cause.
Treat the underlying blood loss
Correct. Hemorrhage is an example cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and the principle is to treat the underlying condition, the real diagnosis.
Start midodrine for neurogenic syncope
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; his brisk heart rate rise shows an intact autonomic reflex and a volume cause.
Start fludrocortisone for fluid
Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome and is not a substitute for correcting the blood loss itself.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes fainted after walking to the bathroom. Supine she is 146/84 with a heart rate of 70; after 3 minutes standing she is 118/70 with a heart rate of 72. What does her heart rate response indicate?
opts: Volume depletion is the cause
Volume depletion is usually accompanied by a significant compensatory heart rate rise, which she does not show.
An arrhythmia is present
An arrhythmia is suggested by abrupt collapse with palpitations and is shown on an electrocardiogram, not by a flat heart rate response.
The autonomic response has failed
Correct. A pressure fall with only a minimal heart rate rise means the sympathetic reflex is not compensating, which favors neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
The autonomic response is intact
An intact response produces a significant heart rate rise as pressure falls, as seen with volume loss; hers rose by only 2 beats.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set1.q: A 3-year-old boy has his pressure recorded at a well visit, and a new staff member flags it as low by comparing it with an adult's normal range. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Measure it again in adult units
The units are not the issue; the reference range is, because norms change with age.
Compare it with norms for his age
Correct. Blood pressure norms are affected by age, so a child's reading is judged against the normal range for his age rather than an adult's.
Start a vasopressor for hypotension
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care, and a reading has not yet been shown to be low for his age.
Order an echocardiogram at once
Echocardiography evaluates structural heart disease; the first step is judging the reading against age-specific norms.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 35-year-old man has fainted twice, each time with warmth and nausea beforehand and quick recovery. Which part of his evaluation is most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
opts: A stress test
A stress test belongs to the arrhythmia work-up of cardiogenic syncope, not the diagnosis of reflex syncope.
The history
Correct. History is the most important portion of diagnosing reflex syncope, summed up as history, history, history, supported by a log of episodes.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is listed for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and has a sensitivity of only about 40%.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography is for structural cardiogenic syncope; a reflex faint with a prodrome is diagnosed from the history.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: A 72-year-old man's electrocardiogram shows runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia after an abrupt faint preceded by palpitations. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Neurology consultation
Neurologic input suits autonomic failure or suspected seizure; an arrhythmic faint is referred to cardiology.
Endocrinology referral
Endocrine disease such as diabetes causes neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, not a ventricular arrhythmia.
Physical therapy referral
Physical therapy has no listed role in cardiogenic syncope, whose work-up pairs cardiac testing with cardiology.
Cardiology consultation
Correct. Every type of cardiogenic syncope, arrhythmic, structural and vascular, lists cardiology consultation alongside its tests.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: A 71-year-old man had his diuretic dose increased 10 days ago. He now has lightheadedness on standing, a 28 mmHg systolic fall and a heart rate rise from 70 to 94. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Start midodrine for the pressure
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope. Here the cause is a medication, which is reduced rather than counteracted with another drug.
Start fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and retains salt and water; it does not address the diuretic.
Add droxidopa as an adjunct
Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is used as an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone, not to offset a diuretic side effect.
Reduce the recently increased diuretic
Correct. The offending agent is removed first: iatrogenic hypotension is treated by reducing or removing the medication, with slow position changes meanwhile.

set2.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set2.q: A 79-year-old woman with cardiomyopathy has had pressures around 92/58 for many months. She has intermittent lightheadedness that comes and goes. How is her hypotension best classified?
opts: Long-lasting acute infectious hypotension
Infection from bacteremia to septic shock causes long-lasting acute hypotension, not months of waxing symptoms.
Acute reflex hypotension
Reflex hypotension is triggered and transient, not a pressure that runs low for months.
Chronic cardiogenic hypotension
Correct. Cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction heart failure produce chronic hypotension, which waxes and wanes and is intermittently symptomatic.
Acute toxic hypotension
Toxic or medication-mediated overdose causes acute hypotension of sudden onset with a specific trigger.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 29-year-old woman with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome is started on fludrocortisone after water and salt alone did not control her symptoms. Which effect of the drug should she be warned about?
opts: Loss of consciousness
Fainting is part of the syndrome she is being treated for, not a listed effect of the drug.
Salt and water retention
Correct. Fludrocortisone causes salt and water retention, which is why it is avoided in congestive heart failure.
Supine hypertension
Supine hypertension is the listed reason to avoid midodrine, which is the drug best with neurogenic syncope.
Worsening kidney disease
Chronic kidney disease is a listed reason to avoid midodrine rather than an effect of fludrocortisone.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: A 35-year-old woman standing at an outdoor event in the heat develops tunnel vision, lightheadedness and dizziness but is still conscious. If her pressure keeps falling, what is likely to follow?
opts: A prolonged coma
Syncope is transient and self-limited, so a prolonged coma is not the expected outcome of falling pressure here.
Supine hypertension
Supine hypertension is high pressure while lying flat, a comorbidity rather than a consequence of near-syncope.
A brief faint
Correct. Her symptoms are near-syncope, which precedes syncope: a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness followed by spontaneous recovery.
A generalized seizure
Seizure is a separate, non-hypotensive cause of loss of consciousness and does not follow near-syncope from low pressure.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: A 70-year-old man with valve disease faints on exertion, and his echocardiogram confirms a structural cause. Which referral is appropriate?
opts: No referral is needed
Each type of cardiogenic syncope lists cardiology consultation, so a structural cause is not managed without it.
Cardiology consultation
Correct. Structural cardiogenic syncope is worked up with echocardiography or stress echocardiography together with cardiology consultation.
Neurology consultation
Neurology suits autonomic failure or suspected seizure, not structural heart disease.
Endocrinology referral
Endocrine referral fits diabetes-related autonomic neuropathy, which is an orthostatic, not structural, cause.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman had her diuretic dose increased 1 week ago for high readings. She now feels lightheaded whenever she stands and nearly fainted at church. Supine she is 132/78 with a heart rate of 70; standing she is 108/68 with a heart rate of 96. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic cardiogenic hypotension
Chronic cardiogenic hypotension comes from reduced ejection fraction heart failure or cardiomyopathy, which nothing here suggests.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Correct. Medication and volume loss are typical non-neurogenic causes, and the heart rate rise from 70 to 96 shows the autonomic reflex is intact.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
The neurogenic form shows a minimal heart rate rise because the autonomic system has failed; her rise is significant.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope is triggered by fear, pain, heat or prolonged standing, with a transient reflex rather than a medication-linked postural fall.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: A 74-year-old man had a faint while urinating at night after an evening of drinking alcohol and little water. He takes an alpha-1 blocker and lisinopril. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Drink less water in the evening
Relative dehydration is one of his predisposing factors, so restricting fluid would add to the risk.
Stand quickly to void at night
Abruptly standing from bed is part of what provokes micturition syncope; slow position changes are advised.
Start midodrine at bedtime
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is not listed for situational reflex syncope.
Limit alcohol and keep hydrated
Correct. Alcohol and relative dehydration predispose him to micturition syncope, and reflex hypotension is managed by reducing or removing the trigger.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 24-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has palpitations and lightheadedness on standing that ease when she lies down. Within 8 minutes of standing her heart rate rises from 72 to 108 while her pressure stays steady. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

Correct. A rise of more than 30 beats per minute within 10 minutes of standing, improving when lying down, in a young woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome fits the syndrome, sometimes expanded as positional.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension requires a pressure fall that meets criteria; her pressure stays steady.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension combines a pressure fall with a minimal heart rate rise, the opposite of her pattern.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear or heat with bradycardia, not a sustained tachycardia on standing.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set2.q: An 81-year-old woman has a pressure of 104/64 at a routine visit and feels well. She worries because it is lower than her usual readings. What should she be told about this reading?
opts: One reading is a snapshot in time
Correct. Each reading is only a snapshot in time and is judged against age, comorbidities and the possibility of relative hypotension, together with symptoms.
Any reading this low needs pressors
Pressors are for the emergency department and intensive care; an asymptomatic outpatient reading does not call for them.
Pressure norms are fixed for all ages
Blood pressure norms are affected by age, which is exactly why a reading needs context rather than a single fixed cutoff.
It proves autonomic nerve failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by one low resting reading.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 73-year-old man has vomited for 2 days and fainted on standing. Supine he is 136/78 with a heart rate of 66; after 3 minutes standing he is 104/64 with a heart rate of 94. What does this heart rate response indicate?
opts: An intact autonomic response
Correct. A heart rate rise from 66 to 94 as pressure falls shows an intact baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic response, which favors non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Failure of the autonomic system
Autonomic failure blunts the heart rate rise; a rise of 28 beats shows the reflex is working.
A reflex surge in vagal tone
A vagal surge slows the heart, as in vasovagal syncope, rather than producing a brisk rise on standing.
A primary ventricular arrhythmia
A ventricular arrhythmia is suspected from abrupt collapse and palpitations; a proportional rise on standing is a reflex, not an arrhythmia.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 75-year-old man with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from multiple system atrophy has supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). He remains symptomatic on standing despite slow position changes. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line for every orthostatic patient and are continued whatever medication is chosen.
Midodrine
Correct. Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope but is avoided with supine hypertension, severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa is the better choice with supine hypertension, which makes it the drug to consider here rather than the one to avoid.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is avoided in heart failure because it retains salt and water; supine hypertension is not its listed contraindication.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 22-year-old woman faints while having blood drawn. Just before, she felt warm, nauseated and sweaty, and she recovered fully within a minute of lying down. Her examination and standing readings afterward are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cardiogenic arrhythmic syncope
Arrhythmic syncope tends to strike abruptly without a warm, nauseated prodrome, often after palpitations.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Correct. Fear and pain are vasovagal triggers, a prodrome of warmth, nausea and sweating precedes it, and it is most common in young women; recovery is rapid and complete.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope is triggered by a bodily function or physical action such as urination, not by fear or pain.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension produces a reproducible fall on standing with a minimal heart rate rise; her standing readings are normal.

set2.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set2.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after taking a large quantity of a relative's blood pressure pills. His pressure dropped suddenly over the past hour and he is dizzy. How is his hypotension best classified?
opts: Chronic hypotension from a cardiac cause
Chronic hypotension comes from cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy and waxes and wanes over time.
Long-lasting acute infectious hypotension
Infection causes long-lasting acute hypotension, and nothing here suggests bacteremia or sepsis.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a postural fall from autonomic failure, not a sudden drop after an overdose.
Acute hypotension from a toxic cause
Correct. Medication-mediated overdose is a toxic cause of acute hypotension, which is of sudden onset, usually symptomatic and tied to a specific trigger.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 74-year-old man reports fainting twice after standing. Before any test is ordered, which part of his evaluation is most important for identifying the source?
opts: A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and cannot replace the history in orthostatic syncope.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope; the history comes first and decides whether it is needed.
A chest radiograph
A chest radiograph is not part of the orthostatic evaluation; the history is what identifies the likely source.
A detailed history
Correct. History is the most important portion of accurately diagnosing the source of orthostatic syncope, or of referring to the right specialty for confirmation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 68-year-old woman with diabetic autonomic neuropathy still faints on standing despite slow position changes. Her standing pressure falls 32 mmHg with almost no heart rate rise. She has no supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat), heart disease or kidney disease. Which medication is most appropriate?
opts: Norepinephrine
Norepinephrine is a pressor used only in the emergency department and intensive care, not for outpatient neurogenic syncope.
Midodrine
Correct. Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope, and none of the settings in which it is avoided, supine hypertension, severe heart disease or chronic kidney disease, applies to her.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is described as best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome rather than neurogenic syncope.
Droxidopa alone
Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is usually an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone; it is favored mainly when supine hypertension is present.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 63-year-old woman has recurrent lightheadedness on standing. Her orthostatic readings meet criteria, but her history does not make clear whether the cause is autonomic failure or something else. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure her and stop evaluating
Treatment targets the real diagnosis, so an unexplained cause needs confirmation rather than reassurance alone.
Repeat readings until they normalize
Readings that already meet criteria do not need repeating to normal; the open question is the cause, which needs confirmation.
Refer to the right specialty to confirm
Correct. History is the most important tool for the source of orthostatic syncope, or for referring to the right specialty for confirmation when it remains unclear.
Start a vasopressor in clinic
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care only and would not identify the underlying cause.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman with vasovagal syncope must have regular blood draws for a chronic illness and has fainted at two of them. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Take midodrine before each draw
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is not listed for preventing vasovagal episodes.
Fast and restrict fluids beforehand
Poor intake and dehydration lower volume and make fainting more likely rather than less.
Take safety precautions during draws
Correct. When a trigger cannot be avoided, safety precautions during the trigger are recommended, alongside trigger avoidance wherever possible.
Stop the blood draws altogether
The draws are needed for her illness; when a trigger is unavoidable, the advice is safety precautions rather than stopping care.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: A 70-year-old man fainted at home and has recovered. His electrocardiogram and glucose are normal. Which tests look for an infectious or metabolic contributor?
opts: Orthostatic vitals only
Orthostatic readings test for a postural fall and cannot detect an infectious or metabolic source.
A blood count and metabolic panel
Correct. Unremarkable blood counts and a metabolic panel lower suspicion of an infectious or metabolic source, as glucose and the electrocardiogram address hypoglycemia and dysrhythmia.
A tilt-table test and a log
A tilt-table test belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and a log to reflex syncope; neither screens for infection.
An echocardiogram and stress test
These evaluate structural and arrhythmic cardiac causes rather than infection or metabolic disturbance.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: A 69-year-old man with a known aortic aneurysm faints suddenly in the clinic waiting room and now has severe chest pain. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: An outpatient echocardiogram next week
Outpatient echocardiography suits a stable structural question; a suspected vascular catastrophe cannot wait.
A symptom log for a month
A log supports the history in reflex syncope and has no place when a vascular emergency is suspected.
Orthostatic vitals and reassurance
Orthostatic readings test for postural hypotension; a faint with a known aneurysm and chest pain needs emergent testing.
Emergent testing in the emergency department
Correct. Vascular causes of cardiogenic syncope, dissection, aneurysm, stroke and pulmonary embolism, call for emergent testing in the emergency department plus cardiology consultation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 70-year-old man on a newly increased diuretic keeps standing up quickly despite advice, and his pressure falls 30 mmHg on standing. If this continues, what is he most at risk of?
opts: Supine hypertension overnight
Supine hypertension is high pressure while lying flat, a comorbidity that changes the criterion, not a consequence of a diuretic-related fall.
A seizure disorder
Seizure is a separate, non-hypotensive cause of loss of consciousness, not a consequence of orthostatic hypotension.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Autonomic neuropathy arises from long-standing diabetes, not from a medication-related fall in pressure.
Syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion
Correct. Syncope is the result of symptomatic hypotension: when the standing pressure falls far enough, brain perfusion drops and consciousness is briefly lost.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from volume loss is lightheaded on standing in the clinic but alert, with a standing pressure of 100/62. Which treatment is inappropriate in this setting?
opts: A norepinephrine infusion
Correct. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.
Correcting the volume loss
Treating the underlying cause, here volume loss, is exactly the listed principle for orthostasis.
Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line treatment for orthostatic syncope and suit an alert outpatient.
Reviewing her medications
Medication is a listed non-neurogenic cause, so reviewing and reducing an offending drug is appropriate.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). Lying down she is 176/96; after 3 minutes standing she is 152/90, and she feels mildly lightheaded. Do these readings meet the orthostatic criterion?
opts: No; readings need 10 minutes
Ten minutes is the window for the heart rate criteria of the tachycardia syndrome; orthostatic pressure criteria use 3 minutes.
No; a fall over 30 mmHg is needed
Correct. With an elevated baseline or supine hypertension the systolic fall must exceed 30 mmHg; hers is 24 and the diastolic fall is only 6.
Yes; the fall exceeds 20 mmHg
More than 20 mmHg is the systolic threshold for a normal baseline. Supine hypertension raises the systolic threshold to more than 30 mmHg.
Yes; any fall with symptoms counts
The criteria are numeric thresholds within 3 minutes of standing; symptoms alone do not meet them.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 77-year-old woman with hypertension takes lisinopril, metoprolol and a diuretic added last month. She has lost weight, her pressure is now 98/62, and she is dizzy on standing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start a vasopressor infusion
Vasopressor infusions are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not for a stable outpatient.
Refer for a tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and does not address a medication cause.
Reduce her blood pressure medicines
Correct. When hypotension is iatrogenic, the offending agent is reduced or removed; her antihypertensives now overshoot as her weight and pressure have fallen.
Add midodrine to her medicines
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; adding it to counter her own antihypertensives leaves the offending agents in place.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: A 75-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction heart failure faints abruptly while walking after a brief racing heartbeat. After his electrocardiogram, which further test helps capture an intermittent arrhythmia?
opts: Cardiac monitoring
Correct. The arrhythmia work-up is an electrocardiogram, cardiac monitoring and a stress test, together with cardiology consultation.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is listed for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not for capturing an arrhythmia.
A patient log alone
A log supports reflex syncope; an intermittent arrhythmia is captured by monitoring the rhythm.
Orthostatic vitals
Orthostatic readings test for a postural fall; an abrupt faint after palpitations needs rhythm monitoring.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 23-year-old woman has palpitations and dizziness on standing that improve when lying down, and her standing heart rate climbs well above baseline without a fall in pressure. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
opts: An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope such as cardiomyopathy or valve disease, not this syndrome.
A stress test
A stress test is part of the arrhythmia work-up for cardiogenic syncope rather than the confirmatory test here.
An episode log
An episode log supports the history-based diagnosis of reflex syncope rather than confirming the tachycardia syndrome.
A tilt-table test
Correct. The tilt-table test is the listed diagnostic test for the syndrome, with a sensitivity of about 40% and specificity above 80%.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 73-year-old woman with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetes also has chronic kidney disease. She remains symptomatic despite slow position changes. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is avoided in heart failure because of salt and water retention; kidney disease is not its listed warning.
Slow position changes
Slow positional changes remain first-line for orthostatic syncope and are safe with kidney disease.
Midodrine
Correct. Chronic kidney disease is one of the listed settings, with supine hypertension and severe heart disease, in which midodrine is avoided.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa is a mild adjunct that is better with supine hypertension; kidney disease is not a reason given to avoid it.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 65-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and numb feet has a 30 mmHg standing pressure fall with a heart rate rise of only 3 beats and no sign of dehydration. What is the most likely mechanism of her syncope?
opts: A vagal surge with vasodilation
A vagal surge with sympathetic inhibition is the vasovagal reflex chain, which is transient and triggered rather than postural.
Reduced volume from fluid loss
Fluid loss is the non-neurogenic mechanism, and it is usually accompanied by dehydration and a brisk heart rate rise.
A fast rhythm reducing output
A fast arrhythmia reducing output is cardiogenic syncope, often with abrupt collapse and palpitations rather than a flat heart rate.
Inadequate norepinephrine release
Correct. Autonomic dysfunction leaves too little norepinephrine released from sympathetic postganglionic neurons, so vessels fail to constrict and the heart rate rises less than expected.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with diabetic autonomic neuropathy has recently begun fainting on standing. She has no supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat), heart disease or kidney disease. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Slow position changes, treat the cause
Correct. Slow positional changes and treatment of the underlying condition are first-line for orthostatic syncope; drugs come in when these are not enough.
A vasopressor infusion in clinic
Vasopressor infusions are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not initial outpatient management.
Fludrocortisone before anything else
Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome; for neurogenic syncope, midodrine is the best listed drug if one is needed.
Strict fluid restriction each day
Restricting fluid lowers volume and makes postural falls worse, so it is not part of management.

set2.io: Define hypotension
set2.q: A 58-year-old man's pressure is 100/64, which is normal for many adults but far below his usual 150/90, and he now feels lightheaded. How should this reading be interpreted?
opts: As relative hypotension for him
Correct. Hypotension is a fall below normal, and normal is judged against the patient's age, comorbidities and own baseline, so a relative fall can be significant.
As normal, since it is above 90
No single fixed number defines hypotension; relative hypotension must be considered against the patient's usual pressure.
As a measurement artifact
A reading consistent with his symptoms should not be dismissed; each reading is a snapshot to interpret, not to discard.
As proof of autonomic failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by one resting reading.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetes asks what she can do herself to stop fainting when she gets out of bed. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Drink less water in the evening
Reducing fluid lowers volume and makes a postural fall worse; it is not listed advice for orthostatic syncope.
Stay in bed until symptoms stop
Bed rest does not treat the cause; slow position changes and treating the underlying condition are the measures.
Change position slowly when rising
Correct. Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, with a pause sitting before standing, alongside treatment of the underlying cause.
Stand quickly to train her reflexes
Abrupt standing provokes the fall in pressure; the advice is the opposite, slow position changes.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: A 24-year-old woman has fainted three times in a year, each time after standing for a long while in the heat, always after feeling warm and nauseated. Her examination and standing readings are normal. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Trigger avoidance
Correct. Reflex syncope is treated by avoiding its triggers, with safety precautions when a trigger cannot be avoided; drugs are not first-line.
Daily midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope, a sustained postural fall from autonomic failure, which she does not have.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not with vasovagal reflex syncope.
Droxidopa therapy
Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is usually an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension.
